raw_findings.message: Adjacent-column checks allow a task in `done` to move back to `review`, despite the advertised workflow allowing only `archived` from `done`.
`parseInt` accepts malformed values such as `"2abc"` and returns `NaN` for non-numeric input, so invalid priorities can be stored and serialized as `null`.
Spreading the entire patch lets an owner overwrite protected fields such as `ownerId`, `id`, and `status`, enabling ownership changes and workflow bypasses.
When the requested task ID does not exist, `find` returns `undefined` and the next line dereferences it, causing a 500 instead of a not-found response.
The default array sort compares numeric IDs as strings, so IDs such as 10 can appear before 2 instead of in oldest-first order.
With no active tasks this divides by zero, producing `NaN` and a `null` completion value in the JSON response.
Compiling the caller-controlled search query as a regular expression allows catastrophic-backtracking patterns to block the server while tasks are searched.
Using `size - 1` as the slice endpoint returns one fewer result than the requested page size and can omit matching tasks across pages.
Task titles are interpolated into an HTML fragment without escaping, so a title containing markup or script can execute when the search result is rendered.
The handler buffers every request-body chunk without a size limit, allowing a client to exhaust server memory with a large body.
Unexpected errors are returned with their stack traces, exposing internal paths and implementation details to API callers.
The server treats the caller-supplied `X-User` value as an authenticated identity, so a client can claim another user's name and bypass owner checks.
The move handler never checks that the caller owns the task, allowing any caller with an `X-User` header to move another user's task.

raw_findings.message: The adjacency check permits `done` tasks to move back to `review`, even though the workflow advertises only `archived` as the next status for `done`.
`parseInt` accepts partially numeric strings and returns `NaN` for nonnumeric strings, so invalid priorities such as `"high"` are stored instead of rejected.
Spreading the entire client patch into the task lets an owner overwrite protected fields such as `ownerId`, `status`, and `id`, enabling ownership transfer and workflow bypass.
When the requested task ID does not exist, `task` is undefined and accessing `task.status` throws instead of returning a not-found response.
The default array sort compares numeric IDs as strings, so column IDs are not reliably ordered oldest first once IDs have different digit lengths.
With no active tasks this divides by zero, producing `NaN` that is serialized as `null` instead of a valid completion percentage.
A query containing invalid regular-expression syntax, such as `[`, makes `RegExp` throw and causes the search request to fail with a 500 response.
Building a regular expression directly from the query lets an attacker submit a catastrophic-backtracking pattern that blocks the synchronous server while tasks are searched.
The slice end is one less than the requested page size, so pagination omits items (and a size of 1 always returns an empty page).
Task titles are inserted into an HTML fragment without escaping, so a title containing markup or script can execute when the search results are rendered.
The server buffers every request-body chunk without a size limit, allowing a client to exhaust memory by sending a sufficiently large body.
Unhandled errors are returned with their stack traces, exposing internal paths and implementation details to any requester who triggers an exception.
The move handler checks only that some `X-User` is present and never verifies task ownership, so any identified caller can move another user's task.

raw_findings.message: Allowing every adjacent column transition lets a task move from `done` back to `review`, even though the workflow advertises only `archived` as the next step from `done`.
`parseInt` accepts partial numeric strings and returns `NaN` for nonnumeric input, while the range comparisons do not reject `NaN`, so invalid priorities can be stored.
Spreading the entire client patch into the task lets an owner change protected fields such as `ownerId`, `id`, and `status`, enabling ownership transfer and workflow bypass.
When the requested ID does not exist, `task` is undefined and the next line dereferences it, causing a 500 instead of a not-found response.
Default array sorting compares IDs as strings, so IDs such as 10 sort before 2 despite the API promising oldest-first order.
An empty board has zero active tasks, so this division produces `NaN` and the JSON response reports `completion: null`.
Treating the user-supplied query as a regular expression allows catastrophic-backtracking patterns to block the event loop and stall the server.
The exclusive slice end is one less than the requested page boundary, so each page omits an item and a page size of 1 returns no results.
Task titles are interpolated into an HTML fragment without escaping, so a title containing markup or script can execute when the search result is rendered.
The server buffers request bodies without a size limit, so a client can send an arbitrarily large body and exhaust process memory.
Returning the exception message and stack to clients exposes internal implementation details when an endpoint throws.
The caller-controlled `X-User` header is treated as authenticated identity, so any client can claim an owner's name and pass owner checks.
The move handler changes a task without checking that the caller owns it, allowing any caller with an `X-User` header to move another user's task.
